title: Stay warm when the heat is out
summary: Pick one small room, close it off and heat only that. Dress in layers, use blankets and sleeping bags, and never heat with an oven, grill or generator indoors. Babies must never sleep in a cold room, and older people chill faster. If you can’t keep the house warm, go somewhere with heat.
doFirst: Pick one small room on the sheltered side of the house, with few windows, and heat only that. Close off the rest (University of Missouri Extension, CDC).
Never heat the house with an oven or gas range, and never run a generator, grill or camp stove indoors (CDC). See Carbon monoxide.
Babies under 1 year must never sleep in a cold room (CDC). Check older people often: they make less body heat (CDC).
Put on layers, a hat and socks, and use blankets and sleeping bags (FEMA, National Institute on Aging).
Can’t keep the house warm? Go somewhere with heat: a relative’s or friend’s home, or a public building or warming center (CDC, FEMA, Red Cross).

list: Heat the smallest space you can live in, on the sheltered side of the house, with good insulation and few windows. It should close off from the cold rooms with doors or by blocking openings (University of Missouri Extension).
Close off rooms you don’t need (CDC, FEMA). Block off the heating ducts to rooms you are not heating (University of Missouri Extension).
Stuff towels or rags in the cracks under doors (CDC).
Don’t open doors or windows when you don’t need to (CDC).
Close the drapes or cover the windows with blankets at night (CDC). Plastic over the windows from the inside also helps (CDC).
Bring pets indoors (CDC).

blocks.p: Any fireplace, wood stove or other fuel-burning heater you use there must be vented to the outside (CDC). Read its topic before you light it.

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

list: Wear several layers of loose-fitting, lightweight, warm clothing rather than one heavy layer (FEMA).
Indoors, wear long underwear under your clothes, socks and slippers, and a hat or cap. Put a blanket or afghan over your legs and shoulders (National Institute on Aging).
Keep extra clothing, blankets or sleeping bags ready (FEMA).
Bed is the warmest place, with other family members and lots of covers (University of Missouri Extension). Not for babies: see below.
Drink plenty of warm fluids, but avoid caffeine and alcohol (Red Cross). Eat and drink regularly: your body needs fuel to make heat (Priorities).
Change out of wet clothes into dry ones (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).

Babies: infants less than 1 year old should never sleep in a cold room, because they lose body heat more easily than adults (CDC). CDC lists babies sleeping in cold bedrooms among those most at risk of hypothermia. A baby with hypothermia may have bright red, cold skin and very low energy (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services; Hypothermia protocol).

Older adults make less body heat (CDC). Older adults without enough food, clothing or heating are among those most at risk (CDC). Even mildly cool homes, 60 to 65°F (16 to 18°C), can bring on hypothermia in older people; diabetes and some medicines, including some over-the-counter cold remedies, raise the risk (National Institute on Aging).
If you are over 65, keep an easy-to-read thermometer where you see it often, and check the temperature in your home often during very cold weather (CDC).
New York State Department of Health: keep indoor temperatures above 68°F (20°C) to protect the very young, the elderly and people with health problems.
Check on family and neighbors to make sure they are staying warm, especially anyone older or living alone (Red Cross).

blocks.warn: Keep the baby in the warm room, but in their own sleep space. Never let a baby sleep on a couch or armchair (Safe to Sleep, National Institutes of Health).

list: Nothing in the baby’s sleep area but a fitted sheet: keep comforters, quilts, pillows and blankets out of it (Safe to Sleep).
Dress the baby in a wearable blanket or an extra layer of clothing to keep them warm without adding anything to the sleep area (Safe to Sleep).
Don’t overdo it: too many layers of clothes and bedding for the room can overheat a baby, and overheated babies are at higher risk of SIDS. No hat indoors while asleep (Safe to Sleep).
Room sharing, with the baby’s sleep space near but not in your bed, is safer than sharing your bed. Sharing an adult bed, couch or armchair with a baby can be risky (Safe to Sleep).

sections.h: When the house is too cold to stay

blocks.p: CDC: if you can’t keep your home warm, make temporary arrangements to stay elsewhere.

list: Go to a relative’s or friend’s home, or a public building with heat (FEMA): a library, shopping mall or warming center (Red Cross). Schools and town buildings may offer heat and light (University of Missouri Extension).
In normal times, find the nearest warming center through your town or city, your county social services, or by dialing 211 (New York State Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Services).
Before you leave a house that will stay cold, protect its pipes: see Protect an unheated house.

blocks.p: No source opened gives an indoor temperature at which to leave. The figures above are what they give: hypothermia in older people at 60 to 65°F (16 to 18°C) (National Institute on Aging), and above 68°F (20°C) for babies, older people and people with health problems (New York State Department of Health). Babies under 1 year should never sleep in a cold room (CDC).

The same rules hold in any building you shelter in: one small room on the sheltered side, with few windows, closed off from the rest (University of Missouri Extension). Anything that burns fuel must be vented outside the building (University of Missouri Extension, CDC).

blocks.label: Carbon monoxide and burning fuel indoors

blocks.p: Power. A furnace or boiler that burns oil, gas or propane still has parts that run on electricity. Oil burners usually have electrical fuel injectors and ignition, and hot-air fans, hot-water circulator pumps and most thermostats need power too (University of Missouri Extension). A generator can run furnace blowers and oil burners (University of Missouri Extension), but only through a transfer switch put in by an electrician: see Generators.

list: Any fuel you have delivered: refill before you run out. Fuel carriers may not reach you for days after a winter storm (National Weather Service).

Oil: dealers advise not letting the tank drop below a quarter. Running low can pull sediment from the bottom of the tank into the fuel line and burner and clog them (Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources).

Propane: don’t run out. When the tank runs out, pilot lights go out, and serious hazards, including fire or explosion, can result (propane safety sheet from Mississippi’s State Fire Marshal’s office).
Natural gas comes by pipe. Gas leaks and shutting off gas are not covered in this topic.

blocks.p: Vents. Keep the furnace’s outside vents clear of snow and ice. A blocked vent can let carbon monoxide build up, and newer furnaces may shut off completely, leaving the house without heat (New York State Division of Consumer Protection).

list: During the outage, unplug appliances and electronics so a power surge can’t damage them (Red Cross, FEMA). Leave one light on, so you know when the power is back (Red Cross).
Furnace stopped during a snowstorm? Check its outside vents for snow and ice (New York State Division of Consumer Protection).

Propane tank ran out? Don’t turn the gas back on yourself. In many states a propane retailer or qualified service technician must do a leak check before the gas is turned on (Mississippi State Fire Marshal’s office). Never turn the gas on at the tank yourself (Propane Education & Research Council). Only a qualified technician should relight a pilot light that has gone out (Mississippi State Fire Marshal’s office).
Pipes froze while the heat was off? See Coming back in Protect an unheated house.
In normal times, have the heating system serviced every year by a qualified technician (CDC).

blocks.warn: Turning on the stove for heat is not safe (CDC). Use fireplaces, wood stoves and other fuel-burning heaters only if they are vented to the outside (CDC).

blocks.p: Each heat source has its own topic. Read it before you use it.
